content.title: What happens when we start rewriting the rules? Is moral leadership in retreat?
content.description: Tensions are growing between national political priorities and international human rights commitments, particularly concerning refugees and other vulnerable groups.
content.extendedDescription:
Around the world, international law and multilateral cooperation are increasingly questioned. Conventions protecting refugees, children and other vulnerable groups are sometimes treated as negotiable. But these frameworks are not abstract bureaucratic tools; they are legal expressions of fundamental human values such as dignity, protection, freedom and the right to life. They rest on an international consensus that may be harder to achieve today. If we set conventions aside when they become politically inconvenient, on what basis can we hold others accountable? And what happens when norms we helped shape no longer align with national priorities?

These tensions are evident both internationally and at home. In Sweden, the Refugee Convention is being questioned in political debate, while discussion of deporting young people born and raised in the country has intensified.

content.title: The right to the right diagnosis at the right time
content.description: Over 80,000 people live with epilepsy in Sweden. Many are children and young people; four children are diagnosed every day. Epilepsy is Sweden's most common chronic neurological disease. Among its more severe forms are LGS (Lennox–Gastaut syndrome) and Dravet syndrome.
content.extendedDescription:
Several rare diseases include epilepsy among their symptoms. Among the more severe forms are Lennox–Gastaut syndrome (LGS) and Dravet syndrome, which affect children at an early age. LGS diagnosis currently relies mainly on clinical observations because clear tests are lacking, putting many people at risk of misdiagnosis or unnecessarily long waits.
Caring for a severely ill child entails great responsibility and can be extremely demanding, particularly with a serious disease. The situation becomes even harder when the child experiences severe seizures and a clear diagnosis takes a long time. This has several consequences for both the person affected and their relatives.

An accurate diagnosis is important for appropriate treatment, but underdiagnosis of LGS and Dravet syndrome is a significant problem. What can we do about it?

content.title: Sweden and Ukraine as equal partners — are we there yet?
content.description: Sweden has supported Ukraine — but is it a genuine partnership or symbolic solidarity? How can Ukrainian and Swedish stakeholders meet as equals to build long-term cooperation?
content.extendedDescription:
Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU) is a project by KlinteVolontär — a civilian meeting place that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

The tent on Cramérgatan is open to everyone throughout the week. It is a place to pause, take a break from the conference circuit and meet people properly — Ukrainians, volunteers, politicians, researchers and curious citizens. No stage. No name badges determining who gets to speak. Every day, there are seminars and open table discussions about the war, responsibility and the future. The tent also has a photo spot where you can capture the moment and take home a memory of the week.

The week's themes: traditions of remembrance and grief, war crimes and accountability, municipal cooperation, the survival of cultural heritage, civil defence, healthcare in war and Ukraine's path towards the EU.

content.title: From north to south – regional strengths and differences in total defence development
content.description: Work to strengthen Sweden's total defence has progressed and is now rooted in society. Yet differences in conditions and implementation remain between civil defence areas, sectors and companies. What does this mean for our resilience, and what is needed for more robust development?
content.extendedDescription:
Innovation, technological development, adaptability, leadership and cooperation are among the most crucial building blocks of strong civil and military defence. The seminar brings together representatives of business, the public sector and politics to discuss strengthening Sweden's preparedness.

Drawing on Totalförsvarsrapporten, based on insights from business decision-makers, we highlight measurable progress driving development. We also reveal differences between civil defence areas and companies.

The discussion focuses on preparedness work in practice, what works and the conditions needed to maintain momentum. Through good examples and dialogue, we aim to reflect ongoing developments and challenge areas where the pace must increase.

Säkerhetsarenan brings together leading actors in safety, security and preparedness to highlight important perspectives and discuss ways forward. It is a meeting place for discussions that help strengthen Sweden.

content.title: Epilepsy: an issue that concerns us all
content.description: Over 80 000 people in Sweden, including 12 000 children and young people, live with epilepsy, a condition that can affect daily life and quality of life in many ways. Epileptic seizures vary greatly, from brief absence seizures and dizziness to major generalised seizures.
content.extendedDescription:
The diagnosis of epilepsy covers several types of seizure, but epilepsy is more than a diagnosis. Many people experience seizures infrequently, yet epilepsy can still affect large parts of their lives. Many children with epilepsy can attend mainstream school, but fatigue and learning difficulties can affect their education. Lack of understanding among those around them can lead to this being mistaken for laziness or lack of interest.

Access to appropriate care, support and follow-up is crucial to quality of life, but healthcare currently faces challenges. Unequal access to specialists and lengthy investigations can affect the chances of receiving the right diagnosis and treatment in time.

The stigma surrounding epilepsy is considerable, and the often negative responses of others, such as authorities, schools and employers, are sometimes the biggest problem. In other words, epilepsy affects more than the person with the condition: it concerns us all!

content.title: Decolonizing Ukrainian narratives: countering Russian propaganda and strengthening Ukraine's voice in Europe
content.description: Russia's information war runs alongside its military war. Russian propaganda shapes opinion in Europe and undermines support for Ukraine. How do we decolonise Ukrainian narratives and ensure Ukraine's voice is heard on its own terms?
content.extendedDescription: For decades, Ukraine has fought Russian attempts to redefine its history, culture and identity. Since the full-scale invasion in 2022, this information struggle has intensified. Russian disinformation spreads through European media, social networks and political discussions, risking erosion of public and political support for Ukraine. The panel brings together researchers and practitioners working on narratives, human rights and security policy to discuss how Europe can strengthen resilience against disinformation and give Ukrainian perspectives space on their own terms, rather than filtering them through Russian or Western interpretive frameworks.

content.title: The fallen of war — how do we mourn and remember those who never come home?
content.description: The war in Ukraine has claimed tens of thousands of lives. How does a society honour its fallen while war is still ongoing? Which traditions of remembrance uphold dignity?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine's defenders fall every day. Behind every name are families, communities and a people who must find forms of collective mourning and remembrance amid an ongoing war. Traditions of remembrance, from a minute's silence to the symbol of the empty table, play a central role in preserving dignity and cohesion.
This discussion explores Ukrainian traditions of remembrance, their historical and cultural meaning, and how we can jointly honour the fallen in ways that do not normalise war but acknowledge its real cost. The event is part of Ukraine's Day of Sorrow and Remembrance of Victims of War and includes a period of silence in memory of the fallen.

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: Soft power in a hard world – can soft innovation power move Sweden forward?
content.description:
In a world increasingly shaped by global conflicts and hard power, how can soft power serve as a strategic tool for Sweden's impact in the transition towards sustainability and stronger global competitiveness?
The programme and participants will be updated.
content.extendedDescription:
History has shown that soft power – in the form of values, knowledge and culture – can be very powerful. Countries seen as credible, responsible and progressive gain greater influence in international cooperation and global development.
This breakfast seminar explores how society as a whole can be mobilised to achieve Sweden's sustainable transition, both here and now and in the longer term. Starting from the need for broad, coordinated innovation capacity, we discuss how democratically grounded approaches, strong collaborative capabilities, creativity and solutions with export potential can strengthen Sweden's credibility and position as a frontrunner in the EU and globally.
The discussion is led by a moderator.

content.title: What can Sweden learn about civil–military cooperation from Ukraine's frontline experience?
content.description: Ukraine has developed unique models of civil–military cooperation during four years of full-scale war. How do voluntary organisations, territorial defence and the military cooperate, and what lessons should Sweden take away?
content.extendedDescription:
During the war, Ukraine's civil defence has been shaped by necessity. Voluntary organisations, local defence groups and the regular military cooperate in ways without equivalents in peacetime European models. Territorial defence groups (DFTG) coordinate with civil society on logistics, evacuation, intelligence and humanitarian action, often without formal structures but with great effectiveness.
This discussion highlights concrete frontline experience and explores how Sweden and Europe can learn from Ukraine's model. What works? What is the human cost? And how do you build resilience in a society not yet at war?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a KlinteVolontär project giving Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and bringing Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: Civilian evacuation in war: what lessons from Ukraine must Sweden learn?
content.description: Since 2022, Ukrainian actors have evacuated hundreds of thousands of civilians from active combat zones under fire. Sweden has not faced this reality, but needs to learn. What does it really take to save civilians when war reaches cities?
content.extendedDescription:
Since the invasion began in 2022, Ukraine's state emergency service and voluntary organisations have built one of the world's most advanced systems for civilian evacuation during active combat. White Angels units have evacuated civilians directly from the front line, including older people, sick people and families with children, under fire and amid total chaos.
Sweden strengthened its civil defence after 2022 but still lacks practical experience of large-scale civilian evacuation in war. This conversation highlights operational lessons: how do you organise evacuation under fire, how do you prioritise, and which mistakes have cost lives?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), an initiative of KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings together Swedish and Ukrainian organisations to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: Holodomor — why is it so difficult for Sweden to recognise the genocide of Ukrainians?
content.description: Holodomor — the Soviet famine that killed millions of Ukrainians in 1932–33 — is recognised as genocide by more than twenty countries. Sweden is not one of them. What are the political, diplomatic and historical obstacles — and what is the cost of silence?
content.extendedDescription:
Holodomor is one of the most extensively documented crimes against humanity of the twentieth century. Yet Sweden has not recognised it as genocide — unlike countries such as the USA, Canada, Poland, Estonia and around twenty others. Why?
This debate brings together members of parliament and analysts to examine the obstacles holding back recognition: diplomatic considerations, a lack of historical knowledge, political disagreement and Russia's active opposition to the recognition process in Europe. We also ask: what does Sweden's silence signal to Ukraine and the Ukrainian people?

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), an initiative by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: The Veteran – an Essential  Resource for the Reconstruction of a War-Torn Society
content.description: Millions of Ukrainian soldiers are returning from the war with experiences and support needs. Providing psychosocial support and using their skills is crucial for successful reintegration and Ukraine’s future. What are the roles of policy, civil society, and Sweden in veteran support?
content.extendedDescription:
The number of Ukrainian veterans now counts in millions and continues to grow every day. Soldiers returning home from the front carry with them a backpack filled with experiences and memories from the relentless reality of war, together with the many skills and areas of knowledge they had as members of society before Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. Successfully reintegrating Ukrainian veterans—providing adequate psycosocial support while also making use of each individual’s competencies and motivation—has therefore become a highly prioritized societal issue, which many consider decisive for Ukraine’s survival as a nation.
What are the key factors for successfully integrating Ukrainian veterans? How is veteran support organized at the political level, and what different roles do civil society actors play? What can Swedish veteran policy—through government agencies and non-profit veteran and family organizations—learn from Ukraine’s work with veterans, and vice versa?

content.title: The Swedish situation – and the way forward
content.description: How did criminal gangs, organised crime and insecurity become established in Sweden? Is Sweden's situation due to chance, bad luck or coincidence? What can be done to reverse the trend, and what role do municipalities and property owners have in this work?
content.extendedDescription: In the wake of recent years' street shootings, record numbers of bomb attacks, lethal violence involving ever younger people and open drug scenes, proposals are pouring in to strengthen domestic security and reverse the trend. Many proposals have a clear ideological starting point, but the analysis itself is often missing. Why are there so many explosions, shootings and criminal gangs? Is Sweden's situation due to chance, bad luck or coincidence, or are there events, decisions or even tipping points that have contributed to this negative development? content.title: Recruitment of children and young people with disabilities into crime
content.description: Although children and young people with disabilities face a heightened risk of being recruited into crime, this group is rarely included in municipalities' crime prevention work. What consequences could this have, and how can people with disabilities be included in crime prevention efforts?
content.extendedDescription: The recruitment of children and young people into crime is a growing problem in Sweden. A report from Myndigheten för delaktighet (MFD) shows that criminal actors systematically exploit children and young people with neurodevelopmental or intellectual disabilities. Meanwhile, a new survey of municipal work, carried out by Stiftelsen Tryggare Sverige on behalf of MFD, shows that children and young people with disabilities are rarely considered in routine crime prevention work. This increases the risk of both victimisation and recruitment into crime. The seminar presents findings from the survey and highlights the need for more evidence-based and inclusive crime prevention for children and young people with disabilities. It also provides examples of working methods that can strengthen protective factors and reduce risk factors, alongside a discussion of how a disability perspective can be integrated into local crime prevention work.

content.title: Crime prevention through urban planning – how do we design out crime and insecurity?
content.description: The design of the physical environment has a major influence on crime and insecurity. Yet these issues are rarely considered in urban planning. How can urban planning be used to reduce crime and increase safety?
content.extendedDescription: Swedish society has changed fundamentally in recent decades, challenging the ability to create and maintain safe and secure environments. One important factor influencing crime and insecurity is the physical design of neighbourhoods, residential areas and public spaces, where conditions conducive to crime and insecurity have, to some extent, been built into many areas. Safety and security have not had a prominent place in the planning and development process. To meet the challenges facing municipalities, property owners and others, crime prevention and safety work must be integrated into that process. The seminar presents and discusses the new BoTryggt2040 standard – a handbook for safe, secure and attractive living environments – as a method to help both clients and practitioners make informed choices about designing out crime and building in safety.

content.title: Goodbye USA, hello world? The new investment landscape
content.description: The global economy is shifting as geopolitics, new power balances and sustainability requirements change investment patterns. US dominance is being challenged and capital is seeking new markets and technologies. How is the landscape shaped as flows are redrawn, and what role does long-term capital play?
content.extendedDescription:
We discuss global investment flows and changing economic power balances. How can capital serve as a strategic tool in an era of geopolitical uncertainty, technological transition and increasing sustainability demands?

How are investment decisions affected when traditional markets become less attractive and new regions, sectors and partnerships emerge? The focus is on how capital can contribute to the green transition, innovation and economic resilience, but also on barriers holding back investment in today's global landscape.

The discussion addresses long-term thinking, risk-sharing and the need for stable rules so that capital is willing to go where it can do the most good. How can investors balance returns and responsibility? What solutions are needed to direct capital flows towards greater sustainability? And how does the global shift affect future opportunities for Europe and Sweden?

content.title: How can research better guide decision-making during a pandemic?
content.description: A central societal question is how research can better guide decision-making during a pandemic. Experience from covid-19 showed that a gap often emerges between scientific knowledge and political decisions.
content.extendedDescription: Research can provide crucial information about the spread of infection, risks and effective measures. Knowledge must quickly be translated into clear, feasible decisions. During a pandemic, the state of knowledge changes continuously, making it difficult for decision-makers to know which measures are most effective. The challenge lies partly in time pressure and partly in uncertainty about the evidence. Political, economic and social considerations can also influence decisions, sometimes preventing research findings from having their full impact. Improving this requires stronger cooperation between researchers and decision-makers. It involves rapid knowledge transfer and structures that integrate scientific advice directly into the decision-making processes needed to manage a pandemic. Overall, the issue is about creating a system in which research not only produces knowledge but is also used effectively. This enables society to make better-informed decisions, reduce uncertainty and manage pandemics more effectively.

content.title: How can science help prepare society for a pandemic?
content.description: The world has reminded us how vulnerable we are to viruses and pandemics. Experiences from Covid-19 show that society cannot afford to be unprepared, making continued research crucial.
content.extendedDescription:
Research is essential both between and during pandemics. Without continuous research, we risk being left helpless when the next pandemic arrives. Between pandemics, we must therefore build knowledge and preparedness. During an ongoing pandemic, rapid, targeted investment in research on the current crisis is needed to develop vaccines, treatments and effective measures, for example.
Ultimately, research is also about solidarity and international responsibility. Viruses do not respect national borders. By collaborating globally and sharing knowledge, we can fight diseases more effectively and fairly. Investment in research is therefore also an investment in a safer, more equal world. Taken together, research into viruses and pandemics is not optional but a necessary investment in a safe and resilient society.

content.title: Mum is coming — but is she really?
content.description: Pleasure is a gender equality issue. When the orgasm gap, childbirth injuries and menopausal symptoms are silenced, it shows how women's bodies are still deprioritised. Sexual freedom is about knowledge, care and control over one's own body. What is needed to make sexual freedom a reality?
content.extendedDescription:
‘Yes, yes — Mum is coming!’ Sounds familiar, doesn't it? It is called out from the hallway, the kitchen and amid the daily juggling act. But when the bedroom door closes, or when she seeks healthcare for her most intimate concerns, is Mum really coming?

Welcome to a panel discussion in Almedalen that refuses to look away. We discuss what is often hidden in a drawer or hushed up in the waiting room. Centerkvinnorna knows that sexual freedom is about the right to one's own body, pleasure and equitable health throughout life.

We explore the orgasm gap, childbirth injuries, menopause and gender-equal healthcare. This discussion is for anyone who wants politics that is as incisive as it is caring.

Come and listen, ask questions and join the movement that puts women's bodies and freedom at its centre. It is high time we talked about equality — including where it is felt most deeply.
content.subject: Gender equality

content.title: What is needed to reduce fatal accidents in Swedish workplaces?
content.description: Almost every week, someone dies in an accident at work. From the 1960s to the turn of the millennium, fatal accidents fell sharply in Sweden, but since 2000 progress has stalled. Why is this? What is needed to reduce fatal accidents again?
content.extendedDescription:
Nearly 50 people a year die in workplace accidents in Sweden. Most are men.
Arbetsmiljöverket's investigations into fatal accidents show that many could have been prevented with the right protective measures.
Historically, the number of fatal accidents has declined. In 1960, there were around 360 per year; by 1975, this had fallen to around 200. This is due to preventive measures, but also to fewer people working in environments with a high risk of fatal accidents.
Since 2000, this progress has stalled.
Last year, a total of 53 people died in workplace accidents, including 45 in the Swedish workforce. A notable feature of 2025 was that several women were murdered at work, partly as a result of the shooting at Risbergska skolan in Örebro.
Most fatal accidents normally occur in construction, transport and storage, manufacturing, agriculture and forestry.
In a panel discussion, we will explore what needs to be done to reduce fatal accidents in Sweden again.

content.title: Women's health: a crucial issue for Swedish growth
content.description: Mental ill health accounts for almost half of long-term sick leave and is increasing fastest among women. This should be seen as one of the Swedish labour market's greatest failures and a threat to both skills provision and growth. How do we create sustainable workplaces for women?
content.extendedDescription:
Women's mental health is developing in a worrying direction, with women reporting increased stress, pressure and ill health linked to work and living conditions. Meanwhile, the labour market is changing rapidly through digitalisation, AI development and new demands for flexibility and availability.

Drawing on the report How Are Things, Sweden 2026?, we discuss mental health, working environments and living conditions, particularly women's situation. The report's findings underpin a discussion about leadership, workplace flexibility, psychosocial working environments and how society can create better conditions for wellbeing and working capacity over time.

content.title: Gateway to the continent or a bottleneck?
content.description: The government recently decided that future surpluses from Öresundsbron will go towards infrastructure investments in Skåne, “in the same way as congestion charges in Stockholm and Göteborg”. But how do you negotiate with the state, and what can it lead to?
content.extendedDescription: Skåne is Sweden's gateway to the continent and Europe's route to Scandinavia. At the same time, the country's largest infrastructure bottlenecks are in Skåne. When the government recently adopted the next national transport infrastructure plan, it also decided to appoint a negotiator for Öresundsbron's surplus, in a similar way to the state's handling of congestion-charge revenues in Stockholm and Göteborg. But what is it like to negotiate transport infrastructure with the government? What should you consider, and what are the pitfalls? How do you ensure that the additional funds do not “crowd out” ordinary tax-funded infrastructure investments, so that local people do not have to pay twice for infrastructure – through congestion charges/bridge tolls and through the taxes everyone pays? What is the best way to remove the bottlenecks? Hear the answers from officials and elected representatives with experience from initiatives including Västsvenska paketet.

content.title: Can Sweden build more in wood while reducing clear-cutting?
content.description: Wood is central to construction's climate transition. Meanwhile, criticism of forestry's clear-cutting is growing because of its impacts on climate and biodiversity. Can Sweden increase timber construction without increasing pressure on forests – and if so, how?
content.extendedDescription: Today, almost all Swedish construction timber comes from clear-cut forestry followed by replanting a single species, mainly spruce or pine. Meanwhile, new models are emerging in which timber from close-to-nature and continuous-cover forestry can supply construction projects with ambitious climate and biodiversity targets, often at limited additional cost. Can different timber types coexist in the market, with some projects using timber offering extra environmental performance? Can demand from construction help scale up new forestry methods? The seminar discusses how construction can help develop a more sustainable timber market and reconcile timber construction's climate potential with forests' ecological values.

content.title: Communication as critical infrastructure – being unprepared is not an option
content.description: Authorities are investing more in visibility and broad communication, but the systems intended to reach citizens in an actual crisis remain fragmented and untested. What is needed for crisis communication to work when it really matters?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden is strengthening its preparedness on many fronts. Total defence is being built up, budgets are growing and emergency stockpiles are being filled, but a crucial piece of the puzzle risks being overlooked: the communication infrastructure that must reach citizens when a crisis occurs. Authorities have become better at communicating broadly and engagingly, with campaigns that are visible and attract attention. But visibility in peacetime is not the same as functionality in a crisis. The systems that must carry crisis communication when it matters, from national warnings to local information in an individual municipality, are fragmented, untested and dependent on technology not always designed for a crisis. Radio, mobile alerts, digital platforms and public service media all have a role, but coordination of the whole is lacking and it is unclear who is responsible for ensuring the chain holds.
This is not just about technology, but about organisation, responsibility and the ability to activate prepared messages in real time.

content.title: From housing shortages to building society – how do we modernise housing policy?
content.description: Housing shortages, increasing segregation and major renovation needs characterise today's housing market. At the same time, construction is crucial to jobs, growth and the climate transition. How can modern housing policy meet these challenges?
content.extendedDescription:
Byggnads presents a new housing policy report.
Housing is more than a roof over your head. It affects opportunities to work, study and live safely. Despite this, Sweden currently lacks a long-term strategy for housing construction, and homes have become objects of speculation and major market fluctuations.

Byggnads' new report highlights the need for stable housing construction across economic cycles, extensive renovation of existing homes and investment in safe, pleasant residential areas.

The report also highlights the connection between housing policy, employment and the climate transition.

The seminar starts from the report's proposals and discusses how Sweden can move from short-term solutions to long-term societal development.

content.title: Young people and the housing market – how do we lower the barriers?
content.description: More young people are being excluded from the owner-occupied housing market. High prices and a shortage of small homes, especially in major cities, create structural barriers. What is needed to lower those barriers, increase mobility and give more young people a home of their own?
content.extendedDescription:
Young adults today face several simultaneous barriers in the housing market. Small, affordable homes are in short supply. Lending rules, mortgage repayment requirements and large deposits make it difficult to qualify for a mortgage. Meanwhile, market mobility has declined, slowing chains of moves and locking up capital.

The question is not whether these challenges exist, but which reforms can actually make a difference.

This seminar brings together decision-makers, leading researchers and industry representatives for an informed, forward-looking discussion of solutions. How can more small homes be made possible? How do lending rules affect first-time buyers in practice? What is needed to strengthen mobility and create functioning chains of moves? And what political priorities should be set in both the short and long term?

content.title: Mice cannot get Alzheimer's
content.description: Mice cannot get Alzheimer's, yet they are the animals most commonly used to understand the disease. Questioning the use of mice in Alzheimer's research is not just about a single animal experiment, but a broader societal issue. How can we get to the bottom of it?
content.extendedDescription:
Mice are very frequently used in Alzheimer's research, although they cannot naturally develop the disease in the same way as humans. Researchers therefore modify their genes so they develop certain brain changes resembling those in humans. This creates an artificial model of the disease. Yet many treatments that worked in mice subsequently failed in human studies.
This raises an important societal question: why are animals used in research when results are often difficult to transfer to humans? The issue concerns both scientific reliability and ethics. If research models do not reflect human diseases, substantial resources risk being spent on methods that do not lead to effective treatments. Animal experiments also cause animals suffering. It is therefore important to discuss whether current research methods are the most effective and ethically defensible, or whether more resources should be invested in alternatives
content.subject: Research

content.title: Regional innovation systems: the foundation of Sweden's competitiveness
content.description: Sweden's competitiveness is created in regional innovation systems, where knowledge, capital and skills circulate between companies, universities and the public sector. In Skåne, research strengths underpin a strong life sciences innovation system. How can it be given the best possible conditions?
content.extendedDescription: Sweden's competitiveness is created in regional innovation systems. This is where companies, universities, test environments and the public sector meet, and where research becomes jobs, exports and solutions to societal challenges. Research on clusters and regional innovation systems shows that innovation largely emerges in geographically concentrated environments where knowledge, capital and skills circulate between participants. This is perhaps most evident in life sciences. Using concrete examples from Skåne, we show how research strengths have developed into innovation systems, how conditions for businesses have been improved, and what is needed for the systems to strengthen and grow. We also show how the European Commission's proposal for National and Regional Partnership Plans (NRPP) could support or undermine regional innovation systems across Sweden.
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: Self-driving buses on Gotland — the mobility of the future?
content.description: Meeting climate targets requires new solutions for sustainable, accessible transport. How can self-driving buses contribute to future mobility in Sweden and on Gotland?
content.extendedDescription:
Can self-driving buses become part of future solutions for sustainable, accessible transport? How can new technology strengthen public transport, improve accessibility and create new opportunities for residents and visitors, on Gotland and elsewhere in Sweden?

During Almedalsveckan, you can experience and explore a self-driving bus that has already operated in Linköping for several years. Come and see the technology up close and ask the experts on site questions.

Like many other places, Gotland has specific conditions, needs and challenges. Together, we want to explore how new transport opportunities can affect more parts of society than travel itself. We will look beyond legislation, funding and technology and discuss the changes we can anticipate and the functions and opportunities we want future transport to create. How are accessibility, services, meeting places and everyday life affected when new ways of travelling become possible?
content.subject: Climate/environment

content.title: How to solve the skills crisis – time for a ministry for skills provision?
content.description: Skills shortages are among businesses' greatest obstacles to growth. Yet responsibility for education, the labour market and business is split between different ministries and government agencies. This hampers coordination and implementation.

content.title: Digital vulnerability – are Swedish media naive?
content.description: The Swedish media industry is structurally dependent on major American tech platforms. This is efficient and, in many cases, technically necessary. But it also creates a vulnerability that could threaten the industry's independence.
content.extendedDescription:
Developments in the USA's global relations raise legitimate questions about trust in American services and have prompted growing calls in Brussels for greater investment in European digital solutions, known as digital sovereignty.

How can Swedish media deliver news without interference from government agencies, political leaders or commercial actors? Should Swedish media do more to build preparedness that works across multiple systems and cloud providers? Are we naive, or can we safely stay the course?

We will discuss this with a number of media industry experts and representatives of technology solutions.

content.title: There is chaos in my head — living with mental ill health
content.description: Am I included in society even if I do not produce? Am I allowed space, and who decides how much? Does everyone have equal rights, or do the conditions differ?
content.extendedDescription:
Welcome to theatre with conversation:
- My everyday life is blank, or black, or full of conflicting impressions. I navigate without a map and usually get lost.
Once I thought I had found my way, because I trusted the wrong person. It did not go well.

My greatest dream is to have a completely ordinary day.

‘Wake up after a good night's sleep, say goodbye to the little ones, go to work and then home to make dinner before everyone's evening activities begin. Then a calm bedtime with happy, contented children before I get some time to myself with my partner.’

This only happens in my dreams. I am alone, afraid and vulnerable. Usually completely at others' mercy. The pain fills my whole body, and worst of all is the shame of being a failure, unwanted and rejected. My thoughts brush against the unmentionable, but hope lingers that there is help for me. Someone who understands and sees me as I am, and makes me visible again. Help me find that, and the courage to accept it. To dare to believe that I, too, am worth it.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: How Sweden can become the EU's hub for circular industry with AI and digital product passports
content.description: Starting in 2027, the EU requires digital product passports. Together with the AI transition, these could drive circular value chains and strengthen Sweden's competitiveness. But are we ready – and which standards, incentives and actors are needed to enable both small and large companies to keep up?
content.extendedDescription:
The EU will soon introduce digital product passports for products with a substantial environmental and resource impact. The rollout starts with batteries, followed by textiles, furniture and more product categories. For many companies, this entails an extensive transition. Data on materials, climate impact and product lifecycles must be traceable throughout the value chain and shared between different actors and IT systems. For policymakers, this is an opportunity to strengthen transparency, resource efficiency and competitiveness in Swedish industry.

Meanwhile, a rapid AI transition is under way, in which structured, reliable and traceable data are the prerequisite for AI's full potential.

Many are now asking: How can regulatory compliance and AI transformation create synergies that strengthen Swedish competitiveness? Which standards, actors and incentives are needed to enable circular resource flows? How can policymakers create conditions that allow companies of all sizes to participate?
content.subject: Sustainability
speakerTitles: Head of Standards and Chair of the DPP EU Standard

content.title: Innovation as a force for transition: can we afford to think long term?
content.description: Major innovation initiatives are central to bringing together Sweden's innovative strength and building society's capacity and capabilities for a competitive transition over the long term. But can we afford to take a long-term view in difficult times, or will failing to do so cost us?
content.extendedDescription:
Innovation underpins Sweden's development and the future society and competitiveness we want and need.
Early results from the Impact Innovation initiative show that its five programmes are now well on their way to creating both breakthrough innovations and the conditions for society to adopt them.

At the seminar, programme directors for Net Zero Industry, ShiftSweden, SustainGov, Swedish Metals and Minerals, and Water Wise Societies discuss the strengths and weaknesses of this unique initiative that is taking the lead and showing the way. How are they working to enable an inclusive societal transition and a sustainable, competitive Sweden? How do we build a long-term perspective here and now, and what are we willing to pay for it? How can innovation make a difference as a source of learning and a resource to be shared, scaled up and used by everyone? How do we build a long-term perspective here and now, and what are we willing to pay for it?
content.subject: Innovation

content.title: What do children do in prison?
content.description: The issue that has attracted the most attention in criminal justice debate and among the public is lowering the age of criminal responsibility so that fourteen-year-old children can be remanded in custody and imprisoned. But what will children do in prison, and what happens when they leave?
content.extendedDescription:
How can the agency carry out this task while maintaining a children's rights perspective? Under the Convention on the Rights of the Child, children have a right to development – even if they are held on remand for a long time and sentenced to prison. Children must attend school and have meaningful leisure time, and ultimately their development should enable them to leave Kriminalvården rehabilitated and safe for themselves and society.

We are now bringing together a number of people to discuss how to do the best we can for these children. When the worst has happened, we all need to help.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.description: As great powers' global influence is rapidly redistributed, a country's image – its reputation, values and international trust – becomes increasingly decisive. What does it mean when soft power becomes a strategic asset amid growing security tensions?
content.extendedDescription:
During 2025, the USA lost ground in global reputation while China strengthened its position. Sweden, however, continues to rank highly among international audiences despite its limited size, according to the Global Soft Power Index.

• How changes in the global reputations of the USA and China affect the international balance of power
• Opportunities created when Sweden is seen as credible, stable and innovative
• How our international reputation can strengthen Swedish resilience, diplomacy and competitiveness
• How smaller states can use soft power in a turbulent world

content.description: In a time of geopolitical unrest and an approaching election, stronger preparedness and greater competitiveness are highly relevant. content.title: Sweden's competitiveness is at stake – how we can win the global race
content.description: China is growing economically, the USA is embracing protectionism and Europe suffers from low growth. As an export-dependent country, Sweden must compete harder, develop faster and strengthen its competitiveness through 2035.
content.extendedDescription:
China is strengthening its position as an economic and industrial powerhouse, the USA is moving towards greater protectionism and Europe is marked by low growth and internal indecision. For Sweden, a small, export-dependent country, there is only one way forward: to compete harder, develop faster and take leading positions in an increasingly tough global arena. What strengths must Sweden build on to secure its competitiveness through 2035?

In this seminar, Per Schlingman speaks with Linda Fagerlund, CEO of Danske Bank Sverige, and Lars Herlitz, Lyten's founder and chair, about Sweden's strategic choices in a new world order. The discussion examines the risks of complacent, uniform political priorities and asks an uncomfortable but necessary question: what is Sweden's long-term plan, really?

content.title: Political advertising in transition – how are democracy's rules affected?
content.description: New transparency and technology requirements are emerging for political advertising. How do we ensure open, safe and inclusive democratic debate amid rapid change and under the EU's new political advertising regulation?
content.extendedDescription:
Ahead of the 2026 election year, Sweden faces a perfect storm: the EU's new regulation on transparency in political advertising (TTPA), tech platforms' decisions to stop or restrict political ads, growing threats of foreign interference and increasing debate about AI-generated content.

This seminar brings stakeholders together to discuss how to ensure open, safe and inclusive democratic debate amid rapid change.

content.title: The year 2040: how Sweden became a growth miracle
content.description: Sweden faces major societal changes between now and 2040. Meeting these challenges requires a long-term approach, new ideas and a shared vision of how to build Sweden's prosperity. Pension capital is a central part of the economy's backbone; how do we ensure it remains so?
content.extendedDescription:
The seminar brings together representatives of politics, academia and business for a forward-looking discussion about the forces that will shape Sweden's prosperity up to 2040. The discussion starts with demographic developments, as a growing proportion of older people and a shrinking workforce put pressure on the welfare model and call for new strategies to meet labour and skills needs. At the same time, AI and other technological leaps are transforming both the labour market and productivity, raising questions about how best to use technology to strengthen growth and security.

A central theme is the importance of a long-term approach to economic policy and the role pension capital plays as a stabilising, strategic asset for the country. How can this capital continue to contribute to investment, development and robustness in a time of rapid change? What visions and choices are needed today for Sweden to stand strong in 2040?

content.title: Greenwashing or greenhushing – do the new rules threaten companies' sustainability communications?
content.description: How do we ensure that new rules against misleading sustainability claims strengthen consumer protection without companies falling silent about their sustainability work?
content.extendedDescription:
As the EU directive on empowering consumers for the green transition is implemented in Swedish law, requirements for how companies may communicate about sustainability are being tightened. The aim is clear: to stop greenwashing and give consumers better information. But do we risk creating a new problem at the same time?

As uncertainty over what may be said increases, companies may end up saying less, not more, about their sustainability work, and may also choose not to invest in it. Are we moving from greenwashing to greenhushing? What does this mean for consumers' access to information, companies' capacity for innovation and the green transition as a whole?

content.title: How long is an arm?
content.description: Both politicians and visitors attempt to influence cultural content. Politicians' attempts breach the arm's-length principle and create an environment where visitors consider it acceptable to do the same. How does this affect culture?
content.extendedDescription:
The arm's-length principle between culture and politics is well established in Sweden. Yet three in ten public library directors believe elected politicians show insufficient respect for it (Biblioteksbladet no. 1, 2026). Politicians also attempt to influence library programmes, which art receives funding and what is staged across Sweden.

In this conversation, we discuss what the arm's-length principle means and what happens to culture and its workers when it is not upheld. And what is the role of politics when the principle is challenged?
content.subject: Culture

content.title: Can your morning swim reduce Gotland's water shortage?
content.description: A shower uses an average of 60 litres of water. When visitor numbers on Gotland peak, pressure increases on an island facing water shortages. Water is vital, both on Gotland and globally. How can we encourage more people to replace their morning shower with a dip in the sea?
content.extendedDescription:
Why shower alone when you can swim together? Every morning during Almedalsveckan, between 8–10, Region Gotland and WaterAid invite you to a shared morning swim at Kallis to highlight Gotland's water shortage and the importance of sustainable water use. WaterAid works in some of the world's most vulnerable areas to ensure that everyone has access to clean water, toilets and hygiene.
During the week, visitors are encouraged to swim and receive a ‘Badborgarmärke’ badge, meet experts who explore water issues from both local and global perspectives, and make the biggest ‘splash’. The organisers provide outdoor soap to borrow and coffee after the swim. Bring your own towel and swimwear.
By taking part, everyone can help reduce water consumption while getting a refreshing start to the day.
But how many Almedalen visitors and local residents will dare to take a dip in the waves?
content.subject: Sustainability

content.title: Can your morning swim reduce Gotland's water shortage?
content.description: A shower uses an average of 60 litres of water. When visitor numbers on Gotland peak, pressure increases on an island facing water shortages. Water is vital, both on Gotland and globally. How can we encourage more people to replace their morning shower with a dip in the sea?
content.extendedDescription:
Why shower alone when you can swim together? Every morning during Almedalsveckan, between 8–10, Region Gotland and WaterAid invite you to a shared morning swim at Kallis to highlight Gotland's water shortage and the importance of sustainable water use. content.title: Weight-loss medicines are changing purchasing behaviour – what does this mean for retail and growth?
content.description: How is the sector affected when population growth slows, competition for customers intensifies and new lifestyle trends – such as weight-loss medicines – change how and how much we consume?
content.extendedDescription:
The use of weight-loss medicines is growing rapidly in Sweden, with documented positive health effects. At the same time, a new study by Svensk Handel shows that these medicines also change purchasing behaviour, particularly when it comes to food.
A panel discussion follows the study's findings: how quickly could this development have a broad impact? What does a smaller and different food basket mean for retailers and food companies? And how should policymakers respond when medical innovations have clear effects beyond public health and healthcare?

content.title: The housing market – a brake on growth or an opportunity?
content.description: Many young people say they cannot afford to leave home and believe high housing costs could obstruct work and study, and even prevent them from starting a family. Why is building and housing so expensive? What needs to change in the rules?
content.extendedDescription: Housing construction costs have soared, driven by regulation, bureaucracy, long processing times and ever higher connection charges. The result is low housing construction, high property prices, expensive rents and long queues, risking both growth and individuals' opportunities. Many young people say they cannot afford to leave home and believe high housing costs could obstruct work and study and even prevent them from starting a family. Why is building and housing so expensive? What needs to change in the rules? What effects do changes to mortgage repayment requirements and loan caps have?

speakerTitles: Deputy Chair of Stockholm's City Planning Committee

content.title: Extreme weather – a personal financial risk or society's responsibility?
content.description: Climate change brings heavier rainfall and resulting floods. What responsibility do housing developers and homeowners have, and what broader measures are needed across society? How are insurance premiums, access to mortgages and property prices in high-risk areas affected?

content.title: Can Sweden afford to neglect aviation?
content.description:
Sweden is an export-dependent country with challenging geography. International and domestic connectivity is crucial for businesses, investment, skills supply and preparedness.

How can we secure aviation's contribution to Swedish competitiveness without compromising climate ambitions?
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's economy is built on international value chains, high-tech exports and a global presence. For many sectors, from life sciences and advanced industry to tourism and services, fast, reliable air connections are a prerequisite for investment and business establishments.
At the same time, Sweden is one of Europe's most sparsely populated countries, with long distances between growth regions. Aviation plays a structural role in regional development, labour market integration and the state's presence that few other modes of transport can replace. In a time of increasing geopolitical uncertainty and renewed focus on total defence, civilian aviation's importance for preparedness and redundancy has also come to the fore.

This seminar brings together decision-makers, business representatives and industry representatives to discuss:

• What role does aviation play in Sweden's long-term competitiveness?
• How does connectivity affect investment and business establishments?
• What is the state's responsibility?

content.title: Building secure, adaptive and resilient digital capabilities for Modern defense and security
content.description: Security and defense are no longer defined by stability—they are shaped by constant disruption, hybrid threats, and rapidly shifting risk landscapes. In this environment, siloed systems and slow decision-making are no longer sustainable.
content.extendedDescription:

content.title: Legislate for defibrillators to be accessible 24-7
content.description: Around 6 000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests are reported in Sweden each year. Approximately 70 per cent occur in or near the home. Yet most defibrillators are located in workplaces and are often inaccessible when they are needed most. There is now a concrete legislative proposal for round-the-clock access to defibrillators.
content.extendedDescription:
BFHS proposes a legal requirement for defibrillators in residential buildings

Branschrådet för Hjärtstartare i Sverige (BFHS) has developed a concrete legislative proposal to make defibrillators a standard feature of residential buildings. The background is clear: around 6 000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests are reported in Sweden each year, and approximately 70 per cent occur in or near the home. Despite this, most defibrillators are located in workplaces and are often inaccessible when they are needed most.

The proposal, Lagförslag hjärtstartare 2025_3, aims to increase accessibility, strengthen national preparedness and create a more equitable, life-saving system throughout the country. Clearer responsibilities for property owners could save more lives each year. We want to encourage engagement and give decision-makers a concrete basis for future legislation.

content.title: The Refugee Convention at 75 – celebrating the world's greatest lifesaver against the odds
content.description: When the Refugee Convention was adopted after the Second World War, the world's countries agreed that people fleeing for their lives have a right to protection. For 75 years, the Convention has saved millions of lives. What does the Refugee Convention mean today – and how do we defend the right to protection in an increasingly uncertain world?
content.extendedDescription:
This year, the world's greatest lifesaver turns 75. It was born in the shadow of the Second World War, when Europe was badly scarred. In a time of darkness and despair, world leaders gathered to answer a crucial question: how do we ensure that people forced to flee for their lives are not left without protection? The answer was the UN Refugee Convention, one of the most central agreements in international law. Since that day, the Refugee Convention has saved millions of lives around the world.
Join us in celebrating the world's best 75-year-old!

content.title: What role does coastal fishing play in the future of Swedish commercial fishing?
content.description: Swedish coastal fishing is at a turning point. Declining stocks, ecosystem imbalances and economic challenges threaten the sector, even though small-scale, selective coastal fishing has considerable potential to benefit the marine environment, local food production and sustainable management that creates value.
content.extendedDescription: Small-scale coastal fishing is often overlooked in discussions of Swedish commercial fishing. Yet it has a key role in the Baltic Sea's future, with today's clear imbalances from eutrophication and altered food chains favouring sticklebacks and carp-family fish in coastal ecosystems. Local roots and knowledge make coastal fishers central to more ecosystem-based management. Selective gear can target problem species or gently harvest coastal stocks with limited bycatch. Small-scale fishing can create jobs, provide sustainable food and strengthen coastal communities, becoming a cornerstone of efforts for a thriving, sustainable sea. Unlocking this potential, however, requires adaptations to regulations, management and other areas.

content.title: How can we stop children being recruited into gangs?
content.description: 93% of the children were already known to public services – how do we stop gang recruitment? How can society prevent children and young people from being exploited and recruited by criminal networks, and how can early intervention and stronger collaboration bring about real change?
content.extendedDescription:
93% of the children were known to the police, social services or schools before they were recruited.
How can society stop young people being recruited into criminal networks?

The seminar brings together police, civil society and other key actors to discuss how we can jointly prevent children and young people from being drawn into gang crime. Statistics show that 93% of children recruited into gangs were already known to public services, and that 80% still live at home and are recruited in their local area. The risk factors are therefore well known, as is much of the knowledge required – but how do we turn it into early, targeted interventions?
The seminar examines how adults can work more preventively, how collaboration between different actors can be strengthened and how we can create more alternatives for young people at risk. What are we still missing? And how can we start seeing early intervention as an investment in children's futures, instead of bearing the much greater costs when things have already gone too far?

content.title: How do we put tomorrow's electricity system in place, for real?
content.description: Tomorrow's electricity system promises faster connections, a more efficient grid and smooth integration of electric vehicles, energy storage and renewable generation. The technology exists and solutions are known. The question is how to scale them up and make systems work in practice.
content.extendedDescription:
Energy and power available at the right time, place and price are crucial to Sweden's electrification and competitiveness. As industrial, transport and new business electrification projects are implemented, electricity demand grows. New generation is being developed while the electricity system changes fundamentally.

Renewable generation, energy storage, electric vehicles and digital controls create opportunities to use the grid more efficiently. But weather-dependent generation and increased power flows also demand greater flexibility, balancing and system integration.

This panel discusses how technology, markets and regulations must evolve to make tomorrow's electricity system work in practice. Energy sector actors, expert authorities and politicians explore the potential and way forward.

content.title: Trauma in children and young people: the right support at the right time
content.description: How can society become better at identifying trauma earlier and providing appropriate interventions to reduce the risk of long-term problems and misdirected measures?
content.extendedDescription:
A seminar in collaboration with Ericastiftelsen on how society can better identify and address trauma in children and young people.
Many young people exposed to violence, abuse or other difficult experiences do not receive the right support in time. Inadequate knowledge of trauma risks problems being misinterpreted or interventions coming too late, with potential long-term consequences for mental health, schooling and life chances.
The seminar highlights the need for coordinated, qualified support in which different interventions complement one another, from early psychosocial support to specialised trauma treatment.
It also includes a panel discussion on how collaboration between stakeholders can be strengthened to prevent young people both experiencing and perpetrating violence.

content.title: Values-driven non-profit schools: why does society need more providers motivated by shared values?
content.description: An increasingly complex society needs schools that do more than measure results, consciously taking responsibility for their broader educational mission and the whole picture. Values-driven non-profit schools put values, relationships and social responsibility first, helping to build trust, inclusion and sustainable social development over the long term.
content.extendedDescription:
Values-driven non-profit schools start from a clear set of values in which relationships, participation and responsibility are central. When school culture is shaped by clear values, relationships, participation and responsibility become central. Making values the primary driving force creates a long-term perspective: decisions focus on the best interests of pupils and society, even when this is difficult.

Through strong local roots, cooperation with civil society and a holistic approach to learning, values-driven non-profit schools can reach pupils who might otherwise be excluded. They contribute not only to learning but also to social cohesion, democratic education and efforts to prevent crime and exclusion.

A school system with more values-driven providers strengthens diversity, innovation and society's resilience: an investment in both today's children and tomorrow's society.
content.subject: Children/young people

content.title: How do we create meaningful participation for young people – in actions as well as words?
content.description: In an era of complex societal challenges, young people's participation is crucial. As trust in democracy and societal institutions is challenged, we need to create meaningful influence and draw on young people's perspectives to develop sustainable solutions for the future.
content.extendedDescription:
How can municipalities and other actors work more systematically to strengthen young people's influence – especially for those currently furthest from decision-making?

The seminar shares experiences from Solidarity4All, a project that strengthens people's capacity to participate. Together with partners, we have developed concrete approaches to increase young people's influence in practice.

We explore what it takes to move from ambition to real change and how lasting structures for influence can be built over time.

Reaching young people who are often overlooked requires new forms of collaboration. We highlight how civil society and public services can together create better conditions for inclusive influence and stronger democratic trust.

The panel discusses obstacles, success factors and methods that have delivered results.

The seminar is for anyone working in a municipality, civil society or otherwise engaging with young people who wants to develop structures that make a real difference. Ice cream is available!

content.title: Prevention that lasts: cooperation between municipalities and civil society across electoral terms
content.description:
When responsibility lies with the municipality, but solutions require more than the municipality alone.
How do we create preventive work that does not collapse when projects end, staff change or election results shift?
content.extendedDescription:
An open discussion on working with civil society to reach all young people, including those in the grey area, and build sustainable municipal practice.

Municipalities have a clear responsibility for early and preventive action concerning young people, safety and social sustainability. Yet many describe the same challenge: how do we reach young people outside established services before problems escalate, and sustain this work over time? During this hour, we invite municipal politicians, committee representatives and officials to join us. Political, strategic and practical perspectives meet to explore preventive work built on structures that last across electoral terms, in cooperation with civil society. The dialogue focuses on practical experience: what often falls short, what actually works and which choices are needed for continuity. Participants leave with a shared understanding of the problem, new perspectives on cooperation and ideas to take back to their municipalities.

content.title: What have 60 years of development aid taught us?
content.description:
The world is marked by crises. Meanwhile, development aid is increasingly used to promote Swedish exports and reduce migration.
For 60 years, we have worked to ensure that aid strengthens democracy and human rights. What have we learned, and how can political work in Sweden contribute to global development?
content.extendedDescription:
To mark our 60th anniversary, we bring together voices and experiences for a conversation about the past and future of development aid, solidarity and people's right to shape their own lives. We discuss how we have linked our political work in Sweden to our work elsewhere in the world.
There will be personal stories, guests and perspectives on the future, followed by anniversary mingling with ice cream and party games. Welcome!

content.title: Fossil-free production in practice – how shared agreements support society's transition
content.description: The transition to a fossil-free society often meets obstacles. Laws, regulations and standards make it complicated and costly, all too often preventing it from happening.
content.extendedDescription:
Join a study visit to Arla Foods in Visby, Lundbygatan 1, and take part in a meeting where we see and discuss how the transition is made possible.

We meet beside the technical solution that enabled the transition to hear from the people who made it happen through agreements benefiting more parties.

content.title: Ukraine's intangible cultural heritage is being erased
content.description: Russia is systematically destroying Ukrainian cultural heritage — buildings, traditions and art forms. What responsibility do Sweden and the international community have when culture is used as a weapon of war?
content.extendedDescription:
Ukraine's cultural heritage is a target in the war. Russia is deliberately destroying museums, churches, archives and living cultural traditions, including Petrykivka painting, a Ukrainian folk art listed by UNESCO as intangible cultural heritage since 2013. The destruction is not accidental: it aims to erase Ukrainian identity and history.
This discussion brings together voices from the Ukrainian embassy, Swedish cultural heritage organisations and nonprofit associations to discuss what can actually be done: within UNESCO, in Swedish cultural policy debate and through civil society's work to document and preserve what is threatened.

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.

content.title: What happens to a person who has survived war – and who takes responsibility for recovery?
content.description: Hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian military personnel carry traumatic experiences from the frontline. Reintegration into civilian life requires more than medical care – it requires psychological rehabilitation, social support and long-term resilience. What can Sweden contribute?
content.extendedDescription:
The war in Ukraine has created a generational problem: hundreds of thousands of soldiers carry frontline trauma that no medical treatment alone can resolve. PTSD, survivor guilt, relationship problems and difficulty returning to everyday life are well-known consequences of prolonged combat service – but in Ukraine this is happening on a scale without a modern equivalent.
This discussion brings together Ukrainian and Swedish practitioners in psychological rehabilitation, military medicine and reintegration to discuss what actually works: which methods produce results, what Ukrainian experience can teach Sweden about preparedness, and how to build long-term psychological resilience among those who have borne war's heaviest burden.

The event is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), an initiative by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Swedish democratic debate and brings together Swedish and Ukrainian organisations to strengthen long-term cooperation.
content.subject: Health and social care

content.title: Integration works both ways – is Sweden ready for its own?
content.description: Ukrainian and Swedish values meet in Sweden – but do they really connect? Understanding one another is not automatic. This is about more than integration. It is about how a country that has lived in peace understands a people who have never been able to take peace for granted.
content.extendedDescription:
This is not a seminar. It is an open invitation.

The founders and guests in SPSU's tent answer one question at a time, asked by anyone in the room. No agenda. No prepared answers. If you have always wondered what Ukrainians really think about Sweden, the war, the future or you, this is your opportunity.

Behind the conversation lies a serious question: Ukrainian and Swedish values have been shaped by very different histories. Sweden has not experienced occupation, attempted annihilation or war at home for 200 years. Ukraine has never had that luxury. How does this affect how we understand one another, and what happens when these world views are forced to coexist?

The unsettling thought: perhaps Ukrainians are not the only ones who need to integrate. Perhaps Sweden needs to integrate into a reality in which the safety we have taken for granted is no longer guaranteed.
content.subject: Integration/diversity

content.title: The sweater of the future – can it be both climate-smart and resource-efficient?
content.description:
The clothing industry is one of the world's most environmentally impactful industries. The textile value chain needs to reduce both its climate impact and resource use.

Can a circular textile economy achieve both?
Is resource efficiency the same as wise resource use in the textile value chain?
content.extendedDescription:
Around 12 kilograms of clothing per person are discarded in the EU every year. Meanwhile, textile consumption increased by 2 kilograms per person from 2017 to 2019.

Work to transform the textile value chain, including raw material production, manufacturing, consumption and waste management, is under way. In 2025, new EU requirements arrived for separate collection of textile waste and the European Commission's new legislation on extended producer responsibility for textiles.

What does the future hold for the clothes you wear today, and how do we need to handle clothing and textiles in future?

Listen to researchers and experts discussing different perspectives on questions such as:

• What can a circular textile value chain solve, and what can it not solve?
• What action is needed in different parts of the chain?
• How do we balance resource efficiency and scalability to achieve sustainability?
• How much do consumption behaviours affect the chain's climate impact and resource use?
• What is required of research and innovation to make the textile and fashion industry sustainable in the long term?
content.subject: Research

content.title: Is Sweden ready for breakthrough technology?
content.description: Global competition in breakthrough technology is intensifying, prompting a historic Swedish investment in research and innovation. Investment in excellence clusters aims to secure international competitiveness and build a resilient society. But is Sweden ready for radically groundbreaking technology?
content.extendedDescription:
In a critical geopolitical situation, breakthrough technology is crucial. Excellence clusters bring together the country's leading researchers and industry's most forward-looking leaders to move Sweden towards international technological leadership. The clusters are intended to fundamentally change how we solve problems and break new ground in pursuit of future research and innovation breakthroughs.
The initiative is jointly run by Vetenskapsrådet and Vinnova. The first call closed a few weeks ago. We are now entering a new phase: establishment.
Does Sweden have the conditions and capacity to take on new, groundbreaking technology? How should we cooperate and think to ensure new solutions and breakthroughs have an impact on everyday life? What happens when new technology meets people and society?
The seminar explores these questions with representatives of business, academia and the public sector. You will also get a preview of strong technology areas in the recently closed call.

content.title: How do we counter homelessness and vulnerability in society?
content.description: Recently, increasing numbers of younger people, foreign-born people, people with addictions and mental ill health, pensioners and families with children have become homeless. Those on the margins are now also affected by reduced or withdrawn benefits, while violent crime involves ever younger people.
content.extendedDescription:
We revisit questions from Frälsningsarmén's panel discussions on Tuesday and Wednesday:
- Evictions of families with children continue to increase. Why is it so difficult to stop children being evicted?
- What does the new co-occurring disorders legislation mean — is it the solution to the longstanding problem of people with both an addiction and mental ill health falling through the cracks and into homelessness?
- More voices advocate tougher measures against young offenders, including lowering the age of criminal responsibility. Is punishment a solution — or could it make matters worse?
Come and discuss these and other questions about homelessness and addiction care. What is needed to create a society without homelessness and vulnerability?
Representatives of Frälsningsarmén will be present: Per-Johan Fernström, Deputy Head of the Social Division; Maria Olausson, Corps Leader/Operations Lead; and Bodil Nilsson, Head of Operations.

content.title: Civil society in development aid – ideological choices
content.description: Civil society has long been a central actor in Swedish development cooperation. Aid is now undergoing a shift in which political priorities, governance models and views of civil society's mission are changing. This brings ideological choices into sharp focus.
content.extendedDescription:
Civil society has long been a central actor in Swedish development cooperation. Aid is now undergoing a shift in which political priorities, governance models and views of civil society's mission are changing. This brings ideological choices into sharp focus: is civil society primarily a democratic voice, a service provider – or something else entirely?
New Swedish research examines civil society's democratic functions and growing tensions in the relationship between the state, the market and non-profit organisations. Meanwhile, civil society organisations face a changing aid policy in which expectations and rules are being redrawn. The government talks a great deal about Team Sweden; does civil society have a role in it?
This discussion brings together ideas, research and practice to explore how different ideological traditions – liberal, conservative and progressive – view civil society's role in aid today and in the future.

The seminar is part of Civilsamhällesarenan.
content.subject: Democracy

content.title: Abduction of Ukrainian children: how do we ensure Russia is held accountable?
content.description: Russia has deported thousands of Ukrainian children to Russia and Belarusian territories — a crime under international law. Arrest warrants have been issued. Yet the children are not returning. What is needed for Sweden and Europe to secure real accountability?
content.extendedDescription:
Since 2022, Russia has systematically deported Ukrainian children to Russian families and institutions — a war crime under the Rome Statute. In 2023, the ICC issued arrest warrants for Vladimir Putin and Maria Lvova-Belova. Yet most of the children are still missing. What prevents real accountability?
This discussion brings together members of parliament, children's rights organisations and analysts to examine what Sweden can actually do — in the UN, the EU, bilateral diplomacy and civil society advocacy — to secure the children's return and prosecution of those responsible.

The discussion is organised within Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), a project by KlinteVolontär that gives Ukrainian civil society its own voice in Sweden's democratic debate and brings Swedish and Ukrainian organisations together to strengthen long-term cooperation between the countries.
