content.title: How do Ukrainians preserve their culture in exile – and what can each Swedish region contribute?
content.description: Around 50,000 Ukrainians live in Sweden today, spread across the country. Access to Ukrainian literature, culture and community varies enormously between regions. How can civil society ensure Ukrainian identity and culture survive in exile, wherever people live?
content.extendedDescription:
A Ukrainian in Stockholm can find Ukrainian books, cultural programmes and a community of compatriots. A Ukrainian in Jämtland or Blekinge cannot. This unequal access to one's cultural heritage affects children most severely – those growing up without access to their language, stories and history.
Civil society has begun responding: initiatives to establish Ukrainian libraries in every Swedish region, with physical collections of literature, children's books and cultural resources, aim to give Ukrainian families a cultural anchor wherever they are in Sweden.
This discussion explores what is needed to build such infrastructure nationally: how can regions, municipalities and library institutions be engaged, and what can Ukrainian civil society in Sweden achieve on its own?

The discussion is part of Samarbetsplattformen: Sverige & Ukraina (SPSU), KlinteVolontär's project to give Ukrainian civil society a voice in Swedish debate.

content.title: Honour the fallen – and what does Sweden promise those who live?
content.description: How can Swedish civil society build long-term structures for cooperation with Ukraine, and why is there still no national platform doing so systematically?
content.extendedDescription:
On 22 June, SPSU opens Almedalsveckan with a ceremony holding two things at once: a moment of silence and honour for those who have fallen defending Ukraine, and an uncomfortable political assertion that Sweden has yet to build the partnership with Ukrainian civil society that the situation demands.

The ceremony includes a minute's silence in memory of Ukraine's fallen. The discussion then opens: what is needed for genuine, long-term, structured civilian cooperation between Sweden and Ukraine, and who will take responsibility for making it happen?

The ceremony marks the start of five days of discussion, debate and meetings in SPSU's tent on Cramérgatan, an initiative by KlinteVolontär giving Ukrainian civil society a voice in Swedish democratic debate.

content.title: When does power stop serving and start demanding obedience? How do I wrestle with my own desire for power as a leader?
content.description: Wrestling with a desire for power as a leader is probably common, but we do not talk openly about it. What warning signs help us avoid an unhealthy desire for power? When does it become destructive? What ethical boundaries and strategies exist? How can a desire for power become a positive driving force?
content.extendedDescription:
The classic question is as uncomfortable as it is relevant: how does power corrupt me?
Where is the line between legitimate authority and a destructive desire for power? How do we recognise when our own leadership turns into control, prestige and a need for validation? What warning signs help us avoid this?

Theologically, power is delegated and subject to accountability. The biblical tradition includes both criticism of kings and prophetic scrutiny. No ruler stands above truth or righteousness. What does this mean when strength is often rewarded over self-examination and religion is even used as a tool for gaining power?

Power changes things! Not only societies, but us as individuals. It provides room for action, influence and responsibility while testing judgement, character and self-image.
How do we use power as leaders and decision-makers so that desires for power become positive drivers and a tool for creating change and empowering more people?

content.title: Sweden lived in safety for 200 years – do we understand what Ukraine always knew?
content.description: The Russian invasion has changed the world order. Sweden rearmed. But have we understood what Ukrainians have always known: that safety is not a state but a choice you must make every day?
content.extendedDescription:
This is not a seminar. It is an open invitation.

The founders and guests in SPSU's tent answer one question at a time, asked by anyone in the room. No agenda. No prepared answers. If you have always wondered what Ukrainians really think about Sweden, the war, the future or you, this is your opportunity.

Behind the conversation lies a serious question: Ukrainian and Swedish values have been shaped by very different histories. Sweden has not experienced occupation, attempted annihilation or war at home for 200 years. Ukraine has never had that luxury. How does this affect how we understand one another, and what happens when these world views are forced to coexist?

The unsettling thought: perhaps Ukrainians are not the only ones who need to integrate. Perhaps Sweden needs to integrate into a reality in which the safety we have taken for granted is no longer guaranteed.

content.title: From words to action? How can collaboration between social services, schools and police develop?
content.description: Recent reports repeatedly highlight the risk of children and young people being drawn into serious crime at an early age. Different societal actors therefore need to collaborate to identify these children early. How can we achieve this in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Preventing children and young people from becoming involved in crime or other socially destructive behaviour is an urgent task for society. 'What Works?' is an interdisciplinary research programme (2024-2029) at the Department of Social Work at Uppsala universitet. In collaboration with social services, schools, police, child health services and service users, it develops methods for preventive work with children and young people in social services and schools. The programme focuses on early intervention and collaboration with practitioners.

During the seminar, researchers and a panel of people in senior positions in government, police, social services, schools and voluntary organisations discuss how new findings can be used in prevention. How can we work together to identify concerns early and prevent children and young people from being drawn into crime or other destructive behaviour?

content.description: Functioning maritime trade flows in crisis and war are essential to Sweden's security-of-supply preparedness. Strengthening these capabilities requires long-term, deeper cooperation between private and public organisations.
content.extendedDescription: Foreign trade is a central part of Sweden's economy and crucial to access to important goods and raw materials for both businesses and citizens. content.title: What world do we want to believe in, and how do we create it together?
content.description: Young people want to make a difference: 86 per cent say helping others is important to living a good life in the future. At the same time, development assistance is being reduced and views of Sweden's global responsibility are changing. Ahead of the 2026 election, this raises questions about Sweden's role in the world and the choices ahead.
content.extendedDescription:
Starting from the campaign En värld att tro på, we move from quick yes-or-no questions to an open discussion about development assistance, human rights and what peace and sustainable development actually require.
This is not a conventional questioning session, but an open conversation between young leaders in civil society and politics about the major choices ahead and the world we want to believe in.

Together, we want to tackle questions such as:
• What future do we actually want to create?
• What role should Sweden play in the world?
• What do development assistance, human rights and peace mean for that direction?

content.title: Tomorrow's decision-makers on Sweden's energy policy
content.description: Energy involves long-term choices for a sustainable, robust society. In an election year, young people's political perspectives are particularly important to understanding how future energy policy may take shape.
content.extendedDescription:
Sweden's energy system faces several crucial choices, and energy issues have become increasingly central to political debate, particularly in the election year. This seminar brings together representatives of political youth organisations to debate the energy system of the future. It begins with a panel of industry representatives focusing on business policy, the labour market and skills supply. These are important issues for the sector and will become increasingly vital to delivering the energy transition. Young politicians can ask questions during the opening panel.

Focusing on the energy system's role in climate, growth and local development, the discussion explores the next generation of politicians' views on responsibility, priorities and long-term thinking. The aim is to improve understanding of the energy system's complexity and contribute to constructive dialogue and debate between young decision-makers and the energy industry.

content.title: Time to step up: how do we strengthen Sweden's exports?
content.description: Sweden is one of the world's most trade-dependent countries, but faces geopolitical tensions, trade barriers, regulatory requirements and tougher competition. Maintaining competitiveness and strengthening exports requires smarter support, simpler conditions and better opportunities for companies to grow globally.
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of intensifying geopolitics and rapidly changing trading conditions, businesses must navigate an increasingly complex world. They also face growing regulatory burdens, requirements and unequal competitive conditions. International trade is, and must remain, one of our most important engines of growth and innovation. Strengthening Swedish exports requires cooperation between business, politics and trade promotion bodies, and a clear strategy enabling Swedish companies to grow in international markets.

This discussion brings together decision-makers, entrepreneurs, experts and public authority representatives to address business's most important questions: how do we strengthen Swedish exports in a new global reality and ensure the right conditions?

content.title: Going to school with anxiety and a stomach ache: evidence-based social inclusion
content.description: The vision of equity and inclusion for autistic pupils in Swedish schools lacks courage, creativity and practical expertise. When schools fail to include pupils, they risk long-term exclusion. How can we create real social inclusion on a scientific basis?
content.extendedDescription:
Every day, thousands of children go to school with anxiety and stomach aches. For many pupils with autism, ADHD and other neurodevelopmental conditions, school is a place where demands exceed the conditions provided. Step by step, they lose trust not only in school and society, but also in themselves.

Despite high ambitions for equity and inclusion, courage, knowledge and practical expertise are often lacking when it comes to supporting pupils at risk of being pushed out of education. When support fails, the costs of exclusion, mental ill-health and future unemployment rise.

The seminar highlights an alarming societal problem, opens an honest discussion about our shared responsibility and points to ways forward.

The question is not whether we can afford to do more, but how long we can afford not to.

content.title: When digital society is disrupted — how do municipalities ensure continuity?
content.description: Municipalities now depend heavily on digital systems to deliver essential services, from schools and care to crisis management and safety. At the same time, demands for resilience, redundancy and control are growing amid cyber threats, disruptions to digital infrastructure and a more uncertain world.
content.extendedDescription: How do municipalities ensure that operations continue even when digital systems are affected or disabled? In this breakfast seminar, Helsingborgs stad shares its experience of digital continuity management. Through mapping, staged exercises and analysis of actual dependencies, Helsingborg has exposed technical, organisational and cultural vulnerabilities, moved from insight to systematic change and placed the issue where it belongs — on management's agenda. Together with digital infrastructure organisations, we discuss how municipalities can reduce vulnerabilities, strengthen their digital sovereignty and build more resilient digital public services. content.title: Together for a good life for everyone – developing a place
content.description: When both individuals and places have different circumstances and opportunities, how can we create a place for everyone? Can collaboration, residents' engagement and a place's distinctive character help us shape safe, equitable environments that strengthen pride, health and confidence in the future?
content.extendedDescription:
For people to want to live and remain in Jönköpings län, sustainable and attractive living environments are needed in both urban and rural areas. In our place development work, "Together for a good life for everyone" means building collaboration, but also creating pride in and commitment to a place.
As we strive for equitable conditions for the county's residents, development based on local circumstances is central. Place development must take place at several levels and involve many stakeholders. The importance of local engagement and residents' participation is common to all of them. At regional level, we develop the county based on its combined strengths and challenges, with a strong awareness that residents' everyday lives and health vary depending on where in the county they live. At the same time, place development takes concrete form in municipalities, where local needs, resources and engagement are translated into practical development work. The discussion features examples from three of the county's municipalities of how they work with place development.

content.title: From global water crisis to Gotland's transition: how do we build Europe's water resilience?
content.description: The UN now warns that many parts of the world have moved from a water crisis to what is called water bankruptcy: a situation where water systems are pushed beyond their ability to recover. On Gotland, this is already a reality – what does the global water crisis mean for Sweden in practice?
content.extendedDescription:
Meanwhile, the EU has launched its first comprehensive Water Resilience Strategy to address growing water scarcity, pollution and extreme weather in Europe. But what does the global water crisis mean for Sweden in practice?

Gotland is undertaking long-term work to address water shortages and develop new solutions for a more resilient society. What happens on the island could become an important model for how regions in Sweden and Europe can meet future water challenges.

This discussion brings together politics, research and practice to explore how local experience can connect with European policy and innovation. How can Sweden contribute to the EU's water transition? How can research and innovation become a competitive advantage in a world where water is an increasingly strategic resource? And what can the rest of the country already learn from Gotland's work?

A discussion about a transition already underway, and how local solutions can have global significance.

content.title: When trust in the media is tested, what happens to democracy?
content.description: As information influence operations and disinformation increase, trust in verified journalism becomes crucial to democratic stability, public debate and resilience.
content.extendedDescription: In an information landscape characterised by disinformation, polarisation and digital influence operations, credible news media play a central role in sustaining a shared, fact-based public sphere. When public trust in journalism weakens, the consequences affect not only the media sector but also democratic institutions, societal leadership and citizens' ability to make informed decisions. The seminar examines how Swedish citizens view their leading news media, which factors drive or undermine trust, and how this relates to broader international perspectives on public service media and trust in news. By relating Swedish insights to international comparisons, we discuss what is needed to strengthen democratic resilience at a time when the struggle over verified information is a strategic issue for society.

content.title: World-class research: what investments and reforms are needed in Sweden and the EU?
content.description: What investments and reforms does Sweden need to undertake in the coming years to build strong research environments of the highest international quality? And how should we act within the EU to strengthen Europe's knowledge base and capacity for innovation?
content.extendedDescription:
In a time of geopolitical tensions, technological change and global competition, Sweden needs both to improve conditions for research at home and help shape the EU's research and innovation agenda.

This seminar brings together representatives of universities, research funders and political decision-makers to discuss how Sweden can strengthen conditions for internationally competitive research environments and take a clearer role in EU research and innovation cooperation.

The seminar is organised by Karolinska Institutet, KTH and Stockholms universitet through Universitetsalliansen Stockholm trio, in cooperation with Stockholm Science City.

The related lunch seminar ‘Knowledge and leadership in an uncertain world: how is Sweden's future being shaped?’ takes place at 12.45–13.30 in the same venue.

content.title: Radical innovation for Sweden's needs – how do we meet tomorrow's challenges?
content.description: Many of our societal challenges urgently need solutions, but some require innovation that does not yet exist: something entirely new that changes what is possible. How does that happen? Can Sweden contribute to the next leap, and is there a way to improve the odds?
content.extendedDescription:
09.00-09.45: Seminar
09.45-10.15: Mingling and networking

If we try a new approach, moving from grants to contracts and from funding calls to a challenge, can we develop the solutions of the future? In this seminar, we explore radical innovation as a way to move from needs to action in solving the major societal challenges of our time. Using examples from Swedish-German cooperation on counter-drone technology, we discuss how clear demand, pace and European collaboration can contribute to innovation that makes a real difference and strengthens both security and competitiveness.

content.title: Climate targets, competition and geopolitics – why is green industrial policy needed?
content.description: Climate targets require rapid investment in fossil-free technology, while geopolitical tensions reshape the playing field. What justifies green industrial policy, and how can it be made as effective as possible? What risks accompany targeted state investment, and what happens if we do nothing?
content.extendedDescription: How can we create green industrial policy that genuinely drives change? The seminar opens with the main messages from a new ESO report, “Grön industripolitik: en balansakt i behov av vägledning”, by Åsa Löfgren and Patrik Söderholm. The report examines the rationale for green industrial policy, how it can be designed and implemented in practice, and how its effects can be evaluated. A panel discussion follows.

content.title: Municipal cooperation: effective solution or expensive compromise?
content.description: Going it alone is no longer a strength. Municipalities face growing requirements, cost pressures and skills challenges. Their own organisations cannot always fulfil the municipal mission alone. Cooperation is presented as the solution, but how do we prevent it becoming an expensive compromise?
content.extendedDescription:
War nearby, stronger civil preparedness requirements and rapid AI development put municipalities under intense pressure. Finances are strained and competition for specialist skills is fierce. Delivering alone is increasingly difficult and risks creating first- and second-tier municipalities.

Cooperation is increasingly presented as the answer, but how to design it to actually strengthen capacity is far from obvious. Contractual cooperation, a joint committee, a municipal federation or a jointly owned company: each affects governance, room for action, finances and risk.

This seminar is for those making strategic decisions in a new reality. How do we build structures that work now and withstand the next crisis and technological shift? When is cooperation a real strength, and when does it risk becoming precisely the compromise we cannot afford?

content.title: The criminal economy – how do we stop the money?
content.description: Organised economic crime generates annual turnover of SEK 352 billion. To function, the money must be able to move through legitimate systems. Cooperation and information sharing have strengthened in recent years – is that enough? What is the next step towards cutting off the criminal economy?
content.extendedDescription:
Fraud against households and businesses is increasing rapidly and generates substantial capital flows that strengthen criminal networks. The financial sector is society's economic infrastructure. It can be exploited when systems fail, but is also one of the most effective tools for stopping the criminal economy.

Important steps have been taken in recent years to strengthen cooperation and information sharing between authorities and financial institutions, including through Polismyndigheten's financial intelligence centre. Restrictions on information sharing between authorities have now been eased. What difference has this made, and what is needed next? How can information sharing between financial companies, authorities and private organisations be strengthened further?

Länsförsäkringar encounters the consequences of fraud and economic crime every day. We are now bringing relevant stakeholders together to discuss responsibility, cooperation and closing gaps in the system without undermining trust in the financial system.
content.subject: Justice/crime

content.title: Energy supply under pressure — what decisions are needed now?
content.description: Electrification is driving rapidly growing demand for electricity. content.title: From invitation to influence: strengthening young people's impact in discussions
content.description: The ambition to include young people in discussions is growing, but practical knowledge and preparation are often lacking. Without the right support and feedback, their involvement risks becoming symbolic. How do we move from goodwill to real influence, and what happens during and after the discussion?
content.extendedDescription:
More and more people want to include a youth perspective. This is positive, but ticking a box on the agenda is not enough. Young people should not be seen as a symbolic addition, but as natural participants with the same right as everyone else to be heard, influence outcomes and contribute.
At this seminar, we present our newly developed handbook for moderators. It is for both organisers and moderators of discussions.
Inviting a young person onto a stage requires preparation. To feel comfortable as a panellist or discussion leader, young people need the right support and conditions. We share practical tips and tools for preparing young people for the stage and for creating an inclusive, respectful discussion as a moderator.
You will also gain insight into young people's own expectations: what they need before, during and after participating so they can contribute on their own terms.

content.title: A regular doctor in primary care – why is it so difficult?
content.description: Providing patients with a regular doctor has long been a central policy goal in Sweden, to strengthen continuity and create safer, more coordinated care. Despite this, progress is slow.
content.extendedDescription:
Today, only around a third of patients have a regular doctor, and Sweden repeatedly ranks near the bottom in international comparisons of continuity in primary care.
Meanwhile, our Nordic neighbours have chosen a different path. In Norway and Denmark, patients have long been registered with a specific doctor, and continuity in that relationship is an integral part of primary care. There, having a regular doctor is standard practice, not a problem. Why is Sweden so different?

In this seminar, researchers from Sweden, Norway and Denmark present possible explanations for developments in Sweden and the differences between the countries. The aim is to offer new perspectives on why Sweden is still struggling with an issue our neighbours resolved long ago, and what is needed to take the next step.

content.title: The role of combined heat and power in total defence
content.description: In a more uncertain world, the resilience of the energy system becomes a central part of Sweden's total defence. Combined heat and power can help maintain stable electricity and heat supplies to healthcare, industry and defence even during disruptions. How resilient is Sweden's energy system in a crisis, and what role can combined heat and power play?
content.extendedDescription: This seminar starts from the contribution that combined heat and power makes to society in the face of threats, a possible attack or disruption, what works well today and what needs to be developed. Combined heat and power and district heating have a unique ability to deliver both electricity and heat even when electricity supplies are limited or other parts of the energy system are attacked, such as attacks on substations and transmission lines, or digital control systems being disabled by sabotage or cyberattacks. Lessons from Ukraine show how attacks on electricity grids and heat production quickly affect civilian society's functions, and how local energy production can become crucial. The seminar also uses hypothetical scenarios in a Swedish context to highlight what combined heat and power can do today and how it needs to develop to continue contributing to Swedish preparedness.
content.subject: Energy

content.title: What does total defence need, and how can capital support the build-up?
content.description: The international situation challenges our safety and security. Total defence needs are growing, nationally and within NATO. Politicians highlight business's role in the build-up. What role should the financial sector play, and how do we mobilise capital to strengthen Sweden's defence capability?
content.extendedDescription:
War in Europe, rising geopolitical tensions and new security threats place greater demands on societal resilience. In response, NATO has agreed to sharply increase investment in total defence, including strengthening civil defence. Meanwhile, Sweden is described as one of Europe's most capital-rich economies, with broad share ownership, strong pension funds and well-developed venture capital and bond markets.

Sweden's defence industry strategy also identifies the need for more private financing and closer cooperation between the state and business. But what investments are required to build tomorrow's total defence? How should they be financed? And what role can the financial sector and Swedish capital markets play in strengthening Sweden's security and preparedness?

The discussion addresses needs, financing and the way forward.

content.title: Prevention, precision and partnership for the cancer care of the future
content.description:
How do we move from political ambitions to real change in cancer care?
Cancer is a global societal challenge. To address it, we must create better conditions for implementing new knowledge, methods and interventions. We need fresh thinking and a holistic approach to health.
content.extendedDescription: Cancer Mission Day brings together leading actors from healthcare, research, government agencies, industry and civil society to explore how prevention, precision medicine, health data and new ways of working can strengthen both patient benefits and Sweden's competitiveness. Through cross-sector discussions and concrete examples, the day shows how the cancer strategy can be put into action – from early detection and data-driven innovation to equitable follow-up and quality of life. The day concludes with the launch of SweCan, Sweden's Cancer Mission Hub, where unexpected encounters drive the next steps in systemic change.

content.title: What are we willing to pay for healthcare preparedness in peacetime?
content.description: In crisis and war, healthcare must be able to scale up rapidly, handle increased demand and keep functioning for a long time without ordinary care collapsing. But if staff cannot manage full-time work in peacetime because conditions are too demanding, how will we cope with a prolonged crisis?
content.extendedDescription:
Swedish healthcare faces major staffing and skills challenges. Access to care and staff is unevenly distributed across the country, the growing administrative burden takes time away from patients, and working conditions often involve heavy workloads, moral distress and repeated demands for savings.
At the same time, healthcare is expected to be central to Sweden's civil preparedness.

This raises crucial questions: how much preparedness should we build in peacetime, and what are politicians willing to pay for it?

Saco Hälso- och sjukvård includes Akademikerförbundet SSR, Fysioterapeuterna, Naturvetarna, SRAT, Sveriges Arbetsterapeuter, Sveriges Farmaceuter, Sveriges läkarförbund, Sveriges Psykologförbund and Sveriges Tandläkarförbund.

content.title: Climate adaptation and cooperation – what is needed?
content.description: Climate change increases the risk of floods and fires. New research shows that climate adaptation is progressing slowly. Risks are underestimated, and damage is repaired rather than prevented. How can we accelerate climate adaptation?
content.extendedDescription:
Climate-related property damage is increasing in scale and cost, while many simple measures are not being taken. New research from LF Forskningsstiftelse shows that property owners underestimate risks and usually restore properties after damage rather than make adaptations that reduce the risk of further damage.
Banks and insurers have considerable opportunities to influence developments. By designing financial incentives for damage prevention and through customer communications, insurers can help steer customer behaviour in the desired direction. Banks can integrate climate risks into credit assessments, loan terms and interest-rate discounts for measures that reduce risk. Such a system of incentives could reduce costs to society and strengthen financial stability.
At the same time, clearer national frameworks, better data and a division of responsibilities that facilitates cooperation between property owners, municipalities and financial institutions are needed.

content.title: From words to action – which methods make a difference to the Baltic Sea's coastal environment?
content.description: Naturvårdsverket has presented its proposal for a national restoration plan under the EU Nature Restoration Regulation. The Baltic Sea needs vigorous action for both shores and waters. What makes marine restoration projects, such as shoreline protection, successful, and which partners are needed?
content.extendedDescription:
The Baltic Sea's ecosystems can strengthen biodiversity and benefit society. Many habitats, from coastal zones and underwater meadows to sheltered bays, are declining, affecting fish stocks, water quality and local assets. Naturvårdsverket's national restoration plan underlines this, which is why we aim to discuss implementation with a focus on the Baltic Sea's coastal environment.

We bring together researchers, project leaders and authorities for a forward-looking review of why biodiversity is declining, which restoration methods are used today, and how governance, increased coordination and local implementation can strengthen the coastal environment. The discussion also addresses the important indirect role of shoreline protection in preserving functioning coastal ecosystems. The session highlights ecological functions, practical experience and scalable methods, showing how stakeholders can work together to strengthen the sea's capacity to recover, restore biodiversity and create lasting value for coastal communities.

content.title: Data centres, the electricity grid and public benefit – how should Sweden prioritise when capacity is insufficient?
content.description: Data centre and AI infrastructure development is now moving faster than most other electricity-intensive parts of the economy. Projects enter planning processes early, with very large requests for power capacity and relatively short lead times.
content.extendedDescription:
Electricity grid capacity is already under strain in many parts of the country, and electricity demand is also rising as industry, transport, housing and essential services are electrified.

Meanwhile, the growing link between digital infrastructure and the energy system makes questions of security, preparedness and societal resilience increasingly important. Data centres are no longer solely about business policy or new facilities – they are also about control over data, AI capacity and energy supply.

When all of society's interests want to connect to the grid, but capacity is insufficient, who should set priorities, and on what grounds?

As a grid company, we see the development in real time: rapidly growing queues in which data centres account for a large share, changing customer profiles and rising expectations from both business and society. Grid companies neither can nor should take on the role of political 'prioritiser' between different societal needs. Where and how do politics enter the electricity system?

content.title: When the world order has exploded

Unrestrained protectionism now replaces free trade, and state-subsidised industrial policy replaces free competition. We are at a turning point. content.title: Algorithms or storytellers – who controls the narrative in an AI-driven economy?
content.description: Those who control the narrative can influence what people perceive as true, right and worth fighting for. Religions, political movements and global brands have all grown from powerful stories about the world and our place in it. But who will shape our thoughts in the future: algorithms or storytellers?
content.extendedDescription: For millennia, storytellers have created the conditions for collective influence. By directing the narrative, they have enabled religions, raised armies and built civilisations. That position is now challenged by humanity's latest innovation, the algorithm, which can map our behaviour, predict our choices and optimise messages on a scale no human storyteller has previously had access to. But what matters most when spreading ideas, products and perspectives: optimisation or meaning? Is it the algorithm that reaches us at exactly the right moment, or the story that makes us understand the message? Who has the greatest influence on the narrative? Let us explore this exciting question about the future together in Almedalen.

content.title: Effective dialogue between civil society and the state – how is it done?
content.description: In a functioning democracy, the state and civil society engage in dialogue. But they operate under different conditions and sometimes stand very far apart, making it difficult to meet. How can they cooperate despite different starting points?
content.extendedDescription:
The state and civil society need dialogue to produce well-supported, informed political decisions. Yet they often differ substantially, both on policy issues and on civil society's conditions, such as funding. Their reasons for attending dialogue meetings also differ: authorities and ministries want help implementing government policy, while civil society wants to advocate for change. How can both sides' needs be met? That is what this seminar discusses.

Nationellt organ för dialog och samråd mellan regeringen och det civila samhället (NOD) promotes and conducts dialogue. Drawing on our new Dialogfabriken methodology package, we make concrete how effective dialogue between civil society and the state can be created.

The seminar starts with a theoretical section on dialogue, then moves into a practical session addressing challenges and proposing solutions.

content.title: Gaza and Sweden's responsibility
content.description: During the genocide in Gaza, society has been shattered, and the ongoing humanitarian catastrophe will have consequences for generations. Sweden has a responsibility. What should the government do, and what opportunities do we have to influence events? What is the situation in Gaza, and what efforts are being made on the ground?
content.extendedDescription:
Israel's attacks have devastated homes, hospitals, roads, farmland and public infrastructure in Gaza. The population lacks access to basic necessities, and displacement, indiscriminate killing and the obstruction of humanitarian aid continue despite the ceasefire agreement.

Israel's actions and the international community's inability to stop the genocide have also shaken the international legal order. The UN Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide obliges states to prevent and punish acts of genocide. States are also required to act to end the unlawful situation created by Israel's occupation.

The Swedish government has faced massive criticism from human rights organisations and broad public opinion demanding effective political, economic and diplomatic measures from Sweden. What should the government do, and what opportunities do we have to influence events? What is the situation in Gaza now, and what efforts are being made on the ground to alleviate suffering?
content.subject: International affairs

content.title: Small sums, major consequences – preventing young people from being drawn into money laundering
content.description: Children and young people in Sweden increasingly face attempts to recruit them as money mules. The phenomenon is difficult to detect, occurs in children's own digital channels and relies on young people often not knowing that forwarding the money makes them offenders themselves.
content.extendedDescription:
Children and young people are increasingly recruited as money mules, for example through Swish. Criminal networks reach them directly through social media, games and chats, often with simple, quick tasks that seem harmless but lead directly into money laundering. Many children do not understand that they themselves can become criminal suspects, while parents often overestimate their insight into their children's finances and digital behaviour. This growing problem shows how organised crime finds new routes through young people and how society urgently needs stronger knowledge and protection.

The seminar discusses new findings on the frequency of contact attempts by strangers, risk awareness among young people and adults, and the potential gap between parents' perceptions and children's reality. It addresses how boundaries and routines can reduce exploitation risks, and how adults can prevent children from entering situations where small sums have enormous consequences.

content.title: How do we invest for the future? Research and innovation as a strategic strength for Sweden
content.description: What do research and innovation mean for Sweden's welfare and economic strength? In a time of uncertainty, technological shifts and global competition, how can government research funding contribute to social sustainability, innovation, competitiveness and long-term growth?
content.extendedDescription: Join a panel discussion starting from the economic conditions that frame investment in research and innovation. Meet the people responsible for all of Sweden's government research funding bodies in a discussion about collaboration and strategies to address today's and tomorrow's challenges. Research and innovation can build new knowledge and generate experience to support well-informed decisions. When global value chains prove unstable and both new and longstanding challenges demand crisis preparedness and resilience, research and innovation can contribute to both adaptation and transformation. This creates new solutions in both the short and long term.
